SOC 2 vs ISO 27001 for AI Vendors

Explainerlowob research

By lowob · 17 November 2026 · 6-minute read · Strategy

In short: SOC 2 is an attestation: a CPA firm examines a service organisation's description of its system and tests its controls against the AICPA Trust Services Criteria, then issues a restricted report. ISO/IEC 27001 is a certification: an accredited certification body confirms that the organisation runs an information security management system (ISMS) that meets the standard's requirements. SOC 2 shows how specific controls performed; ISO/IEC 27001 shows that a management system exists and keeps improving. Neither currently tests whether an AI model is accurate or well governed.

Key points

  • The AICPA describes a SOC 2 examination as an assertion-based examination of a service organisation's system description and controls relevant to security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality or privacy.
  • ISO/IEC 27001:2022, the third edition, was published on 25 October 2022, with one amendment in 2024 on climate action changes. ISO notes that certification is optional.
  • The 2022 edition has 93 reference controls in Annex A, down from 114 in the 2013 edition. Certificates to the 2013 edition ceased to be valid after 31 October 2025.
  • An ISO/IEC 27001 certificate typically runs a three-year cycle with annual surveillance audits and a recertification audit at the end.
  • The AICPA's October 2026 exposure draft adds AI points of focus to SOC 2. ISO/IEC 27001 has no AI-specific controls; ISO/IEC 42001 covers AI management separately.

What the two terms mean

SOC 2 comes from the American Institute of CPAs. A licensed CPA firm examines the vendor's own description of its system and tests the controls behind it. The AICPA's guide for practitioners notes that customers and business partners typically need information about a service organisation's controls and often request a SOC 2 report. The output is an opinion, the system description and the tests performed with results. Our explainer on SOC 2 for AI vendors covers Type 1 and Type 2 reports and the AI gaps in detail.

ISO/IEC 27001 is published jointly by ISO and the IEC. It sets requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving an ISMS, for organisations of any size and sector. The organisation defines a scope, assesses its information security risks and selects controls, using Annex A as a reference list. An accredited certification body then audits it. ISO's own guidance asks firms to cite the full edition, "certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022", rather than "ISO 27001". The ISO Survey 2022 counted over 70,000 certificates across about 150 countries.

DimensionSOC 2ISO/IEC 27001
Type of assuranceAttestation report by a CPA firmCertification by an accredited certification body
Criteria ownerAICPA Trust Services CriteriaISO and IEC
What is assessedControls for a described system, against chosen categoriesA management system for a defined scope
Control setVendor designs its own controls to meet the criteriaRisk-based selection, with 93 Annex A reference controls
OutputDetailed report, usually shared under NDACertificate stating the scope; audit report stays private
Evidence of operationType 2 tests controls over a periodAnnual surveillance audits within a three-year cycle
AI coverage todayNone specific; AI points of focus proposed for 2027None specific; ISO/IEC 42001 is the AI counterpart

What each proves, and what neither proves

The two answer different questions. A SOC 2 Type 2 report says that named controls, such as access reviews or change approvals, operated effectively over a stated period, and it lists any exceptions. It is detailed and specific to one system. ISO/IEC 27001 says the organisation has a working process for finding and treating security risks, with management review and internal audit. It is broader and less detailed about any single control.

The AICPA has published a mapping between the Trust Services Criteria and ISO 27001, posted in May 2018 and available to members. Overlap is substantial, which is why many vendors hold both. Overlap is not equivalence: a certificate does not show test results, and a SOC 2 report does not show a management system.

For AI vendors, the same gaps appear in both:

  • Scope can exclude the AI. A SOC 2 system description or an ISMS scope statement may not cover a newly launched AI feature.
  • Model providers sit outside. Third-party model providers are often carved out of SOC 2 reports and treated as suppliers within an ISMS.
  • Model behaviour is untested. Accuracy, drift and bias are outside both frameworks as written.

The AICPA's exposure draft of 28 October 2026 proposes points of focus on AI governance, model monitoring, prompt manipulation, data poisoning and training data management. If approved, they would apply to engagements beginning on or after 31 December 2027. For AI management itself, ISO/IEC 42001 is the certifiable standard.

Which to ask for

SituationWhat to ask the vendor for
US enterprise buyers, or a procurement team that names SOC 2SOC 2 Type 2, period ending within 12 months
International buyers, or tenders that name ISOISO/IEC 27001:2022 certificate and its scope statement
Vendor holds client confidential dataEither, plus confidentiality in SOC 2 scope
AI outputs drive decisions or customer messagesSOC 2 with processing integrity, plus evaluation evidence
Vendor claims AI governance maturityISO/IEC 42001, or a written answer on drift and evaluation
New vendor with neitherA dated plan, and a bridge of your own controls in the meantime

A short checklist when reading either document:

  1. Check the date and edition. A 27001 certificate should name the 2022 edition; a SOC 2 period should be recent.
  2. Read the scope. Confirm that the product and AI features you are buying are inside it.
  3. Find the model providers. Ask which are carved out and how the vendor monitors them.
  4. Ask for the Statement of Applicability. For 27001, it shows which Annex A controls were included or excluded, and why.
  5. Record what you accepted. Note the evidence, the gaps and the review date.

The lowob view

In the brain loop of store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning, an AI vendor usually supplies part of the wiring or the reasoning. SOC 2 and ISO/IEC 27001 are evidence that the vendor protects what passes through it. They say nothing about whether your firm should let the tool draft, act with approval or act alone.

That judgment is yours, and it belongs in your own record: which AI uses are approved, at what autonomy level, on what evidence, with what review date. As we argue in Regulators Want the Chain, Not the Model, that chain of decisions is what scrutiny turns to. Rent the wiring, accept the vendor's certificates as hygiene, and own the decision record.

lowob takeaways

  • Attestation versus certification. SOC 2 tests named controls; ISO/IEC 27001 certifies a management system.
  • Overlap is not equivalence. Many vendors need both, depending on who buys from them.
  • Read the scope first. AI features and model providers are the most common exclusions.
  • Neither tests the model. Ask separately about evaluation, drift and ISO/IEC 42001.

Common questions

Is SOC 2 or ISO 27001 better?

Neither is better in general. SOC 2 gives detailed test results for specific controls; ISO/IEC 27001 certifies an information security management system. Buyer location and contract terms usually decide which is required.

Does ISO 27001 certification replace a SOC 2 report?

Not for buyers who ask for SOC 2. The control areas overlap, but a certificate does not include the test results and exceptions that a SOC 2 report shows.

How long is an ISO 27001 certificate valid?

Typically three years, with annual surveillance audits and a recertification audit at the end of the cycle. Certificates to the 2013 edition ceased to be valid after 31 October 2025.

Do SOC 2 or ISO 27001 cover AI risks?

Not specifically today. The AICPA has proposed AI points of focus for 2027, and ISO/IEC 42001 covers AI management systems separately.

Next Move

For each AI vendor you use, note whether it holds SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or both, and whether the AI features you use sit inside the scope. Any vendor where the answer is "not in scope" goes on this month's review list.
